hints: Focus on what complete combustion means, every C becomes CO2 and every H becomes H2O, so all the oxygen needed comes from O2.
Write the balanced equation for 1 mol of C3H6 first, it needs 3 mol O2 for the carbon and 1.5 mol O2 for the hydrogen, giving 4.5 mol O2 in total.
Do the same balancing for 1 mol of C4H6 to get its O2 need, then simply add the two O2 amounts together for the mixture.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for complete combustion**

Great start, let's think simply. A hydrocarbon burns in oxygen to make only carbon dioxide and water.

General idea:
$$\text{C}_x\text{H}_y + \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)\text{O}_2 \rightarrow x\text{CO}_2 + \frac{y}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Balance combustion of C3H6**

Look at 1 mol of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$. It makes 3 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ and 3 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Count the O atoms needed in products: $(3 \times 2) + (3 \times 1) = 9$ O atoms. That is $4.5$ $\text{O}_2$ molecules.
$$\text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + 4.5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Balance combustion of C4H6**

Now do the same for 1 mol of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6$. It makes 4 mol of $\text{CO}_2$ and 3 mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Count the O atoms needed: $(4 \times 2) + (3 \times 1) = 11$ O atoms. That is $5.5$ $\text{O}_2$ molecules.
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_6 + 5.5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Add for mixture R**

Mixture R has both compounds together, so just add the oxygen demands.

Calculation:
$$4.5 + 5.5 = 10 \text{ mol of O}_2$$

options.A: Incorrect. 6.5 is far too low and comes from an unbalanced equation, often by forgetting how much oxygen is needed to make water as well as carbon dioxide.
options.B: Incorrect. 7 is the total moles of CO2 formed (3 + 4), not the moles of O2 used. Many students pick this trap by counting carbon only and forgetting the hydrogen combustion.
options.C: Correct. 4.5 mol O2 for C3H6 plus 5.5 mol O2 for C4H6 gives 10 mol O2 in total for complete combustion of the 2 mol mixture.
options.D: Incorrect. 20 is the number of moles of oxygen atoms (O), not oxygen molecules (O2). Since each O2 has 2 O atoms, you must halve 20 to get 10 mol O2.
